semblance

SEM-blunss -- Old French sembler, 'to seem,' from Latin similis, 'like': the same family as 'resemble.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Semblance is an outward form or appearance of something.

After the storm passed, the town slowly returned to a semblance of normal life.

Example

Minutes before guests arrive, a family shoves laundry into closets and stacks dishes out of sight, so the house looks calm and tidy even though chaos hides behind every door.

That outward appearance of order without the full reality behind it is exactly what a semblance is. Unlike 'reality,' a semblance may be only surface-deep.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

facade: A facade is a false front kept up on purpose, the way a building's grand stone face can hide plain brick behind it. A semblance is thinner and less deliberate -- the mere outward look of calm or order, however it came about.

veneer: A veneer is a thin, attractive layer laid over something coarser -- polished manners over rudeness, fine wood glued over cheap board. A semblance is not a covering at all: just the outward look of a thing, with or without depth behind it.

pretense: A pretense is a false show deliberately kept up so that others will believe something. A semblance needs no deceiver at all -- the outward look can simply be there, with nobody trying to fool anyone about what lies underneath.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reality: what actually exists

substance: the real matter beneath appearances

Where it sits · how deceptive the outward show is — appearance → semblance → guise

appearance vs. semblance: Appearance is the plain, neutral cousin of semblance -- everything has an appearance, while a semblance hints that the outward look may be all there is.

guise vs. semblance: Guise is more deceptive than semblance: a semblance is a thin outward show of something, while a guise is a disguise-like false front deliberately put on.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — sembl-

root — sembl-: to seem, to be like (Old French (sembler), from Latin similis ('like'))

suffix — -ance

suffix — -ance: state or quality of (Latin (-antia))

Put it together

Put it together: Old French sembler meant 'to seem,' from Latin similis ('like') -- a semblance is the state of seeming like something, the same root that gives us resemble and similar.

Use the root in a new word: resemble

Use the root in a new word: resemble: With his gray whiskers, the old dog had begun to resemble his owner.

Word Choice

Semblance is almost always followed by 'of' -- 'a semblance of order,' 'some semblance of normalcy' -- and often implies the appearance is fragile or only partial.
